https://www.ebrd.com/home/news-and-event.text: EBRD extends loan of up to PLN 400 million to Tele Fonika Kable 22 Jul 2026 Share Linkedin Facebook Whatsapp Twitter Email Copy Link Author: Nigina Mirbabaeva The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) is lending up to PLN 400 million (€92 million equivalent) to Tele-Fonika Kable, a leading European producer of power cables, to support the expansion of its medium and high voltage cable manufacturing and related research and development in Poland . The loan is being provided as part of a PLN 2.36 billion financing package with a consortium of banks. Tele-Fonika Kable will primarily use the loan to expand production at its Bydgoszcz facility and to develop new laboratory and testing capabilities at the site. This will help strengthen Poland’s domestic manufacturing capacity for equipment that is critical to the modernisation of electricity transmission and distribution networks as well as the integration of renewable energy. Investments in medium and high voltage cables are also essential to improve Poland’s energy security, as the rapid deployment of renewables in the country requires significant upgrades to grid infrastructure. Andreea Moraru, EBRD Managing Director for central Europe and the Baltic states, said: “This investment directly supports the Bank’s two key priorities in Poland: strengthening energy security and boosting the competitiveness of its vibrant companies. We will continue to back leading firms such as Tele-Fonika Kable as they grow, innovate and contribute to a greener energy system.” Frederic Lucenet, EBRD Head of Manufacturing and Services, said: “We are delighted to again support Tele-Fonika Kable as it embarks on its next growth phase and to help strengthen the long-term competitiveness of Poland’s manufacturing base. Grid capacity is a key constraint in the transition to renewable energy. In this context and beyond Poland, Tele-Fonika Kable plays an important role in supporting the modernisation of Europe’s electricity grids. Bartłomiej Zgryzek, Vice President of Tele-Fonika Kable’s management board, said: “The support of the EBRD and our banking partners enables us to accelerate strategic investments in manufacturing capacity and innovation. By expanding our facilities in Bydgoszcz, we are strengthening our ability to deliver advanced medium- and high-voltage cable solutions that are essential for modernising power grids, enhancing energy security and supporting the energy transition in Poland and beyond.” Tele-Fonika Kable is one of the largest cable and wire manufacturers in central and eastern Europe, supplying more than 80 markets worldwide. The company has been an EBRD client since 2015 and has progressively shifted towards higher value products used in renewable energy and grid modernisation projects. The EBRD is one of Poland’s key institutional investors, having invested more than €17 billion in the country since 1991 across hundreds of projects, largely in the private sector, with a strong focus on supporting the green transition, energy security and sustainable economic growth. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.text: NATO secretary general Mark Rutte discussed Britain’s Nato commitments with Andy Burnham during their first one-on-one meeting. Photograph: Neil Hall/EPA View image in fullscreen NATO secretary general Mark Rutte discussed Britain’s Nato commitments with Andy Burnham during their first one-on-one meeting. Photograph: Neil Hall/EPA World news Nato leader warns of ‘most dangerous and complex security environment in a generation’ Mark Rutte asked UK and Europe to ‘provide the hard power Nato needs’ in face of geopolitical uncertainty Dan Sabbagh Defence and security editor Wed 16 Sep 2026 14.46 EDT Last modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 16.16 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Nato needs “more UK and more Europe” to deal with the most dangerous security environment faced by the west in a generation, the secretary general of the 32-country military alliance said this afternoon on a visit to the UK. Mark Rutte praised Britain for promising to increase defence spending in line with US demands after a meeting with prime minister Andy Burnham – but argued that the military and financial effort must continue into the future. “It is essential that your armed forces continue to provide the hard power Nato needs,” Rutte said in a speech to a specialist audience at Ditchley Park, a wartime retreat used by Winston Churchill in Oxfordshire. It was a plea for the UK to make progress towards an alliance-wide target demanded by Donald Trump of spending 3.5% of GDP by 2035, around £30bn in real terms, money that has to be found from extra taxation, borrowing or reducing other spending. Russian warship fires flares at Danish helicopter as Nato jets shoot down drone over Lithuania Read more Britain has so far only budgeted to increase defence spending to 2.7% of GDP by the end of the next decade. Short-term financial pressures have meant that the army has been told to stop non-essential training by the end of the year. Chancellor John Healey resigned as defence secretary from Keir Starmer’s government in June because the former prime minister would not commit to 3% by 2030, arguing that it would require too great a step up in the next decade. But Healey refused to recommit to the interim target when he was appointed to the Treasury by Burnham a month later, raising questions that the new government was backloading spending increases until after the next election. Rutte said that he had discussed Britain’s “Nato commitments” when he had met Burnham at a science business park in Oxford earlier on Wednesday, without offering any details, in the first one-on-one meeting between the two. Prior to that meeting, Burnham acknowledged that he had replaced Starmer, but insisted that there was “never any change in the UK’s unwavering commitment to Nato and our Nato obligations”. The Nato chief, a former Dutch prime minister, said that many in Europe had made the “casual assumption” that the US would “always provide most of the muscle and pick up the bill, no matter what” until Trump returned to the White House. Instead, he noted that during a summit in The Hague in 2025, the UK and other alliance members had agreed to increase their own defence spending to match US levels, in response to Trump’s demand that Europe take the lead in defending the continent. “We need more UK and more Europe in the alliance,” Rutte said, because Nato “faces the most dangerous and complex security environment in a generation” with a return to wars in Europe and the Middle East, and wider geopolitical uncertainty. Ukraine war briefing: Nato ‘foils Russian undersea cable sabotage drill’ Read more Citing “Russia and its war against Ukraine, terrorism, Iran and the tectonic shifts of global geopolitical competition”, Rutte argued that the UK and Europe needed to invest more, because otherwise “our collective defence will not be credible”. Britain, he said, had “a central role in building this stronger Europe in a stronger Nato” and noted that the UK was spending billions to upgrade the Trident nuclear deterrent, which is pledged to the defence of Nato members. The UK is also gradually upgrading its conventional forces, though the UK’s overall defence spending, long the second largest in the alliance, is now behind Germany. By 2029, Berlin’s military budgets are on track to be twice that of the UK. The UK was “leading the pushback” against a Russian campaign of provocation and sabotage across Europe, Rutte said, and that the UK had been “a good friend to Ukraine”. Britain spends £3bn a year supporting Ukraine with weapons. https://www.politico.eu/article/plague-r.text: As whispers circulate of plague in faraway Siberia, it’s worth remembering that Russian obfuscation is so ingrained that it’s become a meme. In HBO’s dramatized 2019 series about the nuclear disaster at Chernobyl, a Russian atomic scientist scoffs at a radiation reading that suggests a major calamity is taking place. “Not great, not terrible,” says the fictionalized version of Anatoly Dyatlov, the real-life deputy chief engineer at Chernobyl in April 1986, as he looks at a dosimeter noting 3.6 roentgen per hour, just below a critical radiation level. Advertisement Advertisement Except that reading was not accurate. Not even close. The nuclear reactor had already exploded and unleashed catastrophic levels of radiation that would go on to cause thousands of cancer-related deaths in the worst nuclear power plant disaster in history. While dramatized, the scene is emblematic of a long-standing Soviet and Russian desire to downplay critical incidents — and even cover them up. That pattern has flared this week, with senior world health officials, the European Union and U.S. President Donald Trump demanding that Moscow be more transparent about a suspected outbreak of plague in far eastern Russia. In dark comedic twist in the face of the potential plague, Dyatlov’s dismissive remark is now ubiquitous. Not great, not terrible. Into the unknown The death of a 28-year-old employee at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East last week triggered unease across the globe due to her laboratory work — and a local Russian official linking her death to a case of plague. Russia was quick to clamp down. Rospotrebnadzor, the country’s national public health agency, said that the employee died from “pneumonia of unknown etiology” and that no microorganisms associated with her work were identified in the patient sample. Still, Russian health authorities placed nearly 200 people under supervision and local media reported that several hospitals were placed under quarantine. Rospotrebnadzor said Thursday these measures were taken due to “the patient's professional activities.” Advertisement Advertisement The World Health Organization, which leads global response to international health threats, got in touch with Russian health authorities on Oct. 3. It requested more information using one of the tools laid out in the International Health Regulations, which Russia is signed up to. Under the IHR, countries have 24 hours to respond to the WHO — though Russia sent its response on Oct. 6. Russian authorities said that “no case of plague had recently been registered in Irkutsk” and “no pathogens of dangerous infectious diseases were detected among any of the contacts.” World Health Organization epidemic and pandemic management head Maria Van Kerkhove, who said "we still don't know exactly how this person died, at a press briefing in Geneva on Oct. 7, 2026. | Fabrice Coffrini/AFP via Getty Images As of Thursday, Russian health authorities maintain that there is no “epidemic risk” in the region. Rospotrebnadzor said that it had concluded health inspections and found “no emergency situations involving pathogenic microorganisms.” It had also completed monitoring of 90% of the contacts, without identifying any infections, the agency added. Simultaneously, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov slammed media reports about the case as false and said Russia has been communicating with global health authorities. Yet the WHO insists there’s still much left unknown about the events inside Russia. “We don’t know exactly how this person died,” said Maria Van Kerkhove, director of epidemic and pandemic management, during a press briefing Wednesday. “We know that she had pneumonia. We know it was a fatal case. We understand that some laboratory tests have been done. They haven’t found the causative agent. This is why we need more information.” The WHO said it requested further details on what laboratory tests were conducted, which pathogens were evaluated, which further analyses are being done to determine the patient’s cause of death — if not plague — along with more details on any potential lab incident and the 200 contacts. Advertisement Advertisement Until those questions are answered, it’s impossible for the WHO to conduct a risk assessment. “We don't yet have the full picture of this event, and we are not able to conduct a full risk assessment,” said Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, the organization’s director-general. “Timely, complete, and transparent information sharing under the international regulations is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public health risks.” Omertà in Russian It might be that the cause of death of the 28-year-old lab worker is not, in fact, plague. But Russia’s incomplete, late and hazy communication about the case is fomenting fears and uncertainty from Geneva to Brussels to Washington. It would also not be the first time the Kremlin has downplayed or attempted to cover up public health threats. That goes beyond the Soviet-era Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant disaster, in what is now northern Ukraine, where the Kremlin was slow to take action and effectively denied the cause of the incident. In 1979, according to an investigation by U.S. scientists, the Soviet Union covered up a deadly anthrax outbreak in the city of Sverdlovsk, now Yekaterinburg, which killed at least 66 people. Officials said the victims had fallen ill from eating contaminated meat, when in reality they had been exposed to anthrax because of an accident at a secret biological weapons lab. Advertisement Advertisement Russia was also accused of covering up a mysterious 1988 alopecia outbreak in Chernivtsi region, in which more than 175 children lost their hair. Soviet authorities said the children suffered from thallium food poisoning, but later studies raised questions about that, with some suggesting the cause was hydrazine, or acid rain . Over the years, the Kremlin has also dismissed , downplayed and underreported HIV cases, even while in the middle of a deadly epidemic . And, more recently, during the Covid-19 pandemic, Russia was accused of downplaying coronavirus deaths, particularly at the beginning. An image taken from a helicopter in April 1986 shows a general view of the destroyed fourth power block of Chernobyl's nuclear plant a few days after the catastrophe, which was downplayed at the time by Soviet authorities. | Vladimir Repik/AFP via Getty Images The tradition extends beyond public health. The 1999 apartment block bombings , the 2000 sinking of the Kursk submarine and the 2014 downing of Malaysia Airlines flight MH17 by Kremlin-backed separatists all raised questions over Russia's public messaging and commitment to transparency. Talks with Putin The EU and the U.S. are monitoring the Irkutsk situation closely, with both seemingly growing impatient with Russia’s communication. “The whole world is waiting for the information from Russia,” said European Commission spokesperson Eva Hrncirova on Thursday. “Russia should make information about the plague available as soon as possible,” she told reporters. “We need information from Russia. It’s linked to the Russian membership in the WHO Europe, sharing timely, precise, exact information so that the experts can assess the situation, because [it] can have cross-border implications.” Advertisement Advertisement The European Commission’s directorate-general for health and food safety is planning to send a technical letter to Russia asking for more information, a Commission spokesperson confirmed. In the meantime, Russia’s “patchy” communication is dangerous, said a Commission official, granted anonymity to speak candidly on the matter. “This fuels speculation into all directions. It also renders preventive [and] precautionary action difficult, if not even meaningless,” the official said. These types of events happen all the time, but there is usually an exchange with the WHO and health authorities, the person added. “The lack of precise [and] reliable info is logically reducing adequate good preparedness.” U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday urged Russia to share more information, adding that it would be “irresponsible” to speculate until then. The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday that the U.S. sent a formal diplomatic message to Russia requesting more information about the woman’s death and reminding the Kremlin that it has obligations under international law to share information about disease outbreaks in a timely manner. U.S. President Donald Trump even said Tuesday he had a "call scheduled" with Russian President Vladimir Putin "very soon" to discuss the situation. But, by Thursday, the two leaders were yet to talk, with Trump noting that Russia was “not saying much.” He still planned to talk to Putin soon, he added. Advertisement

https://bnn-news.com/bnn-in-focus/bnn-in.text: Photo: LETA/BNN collage/AI Advertisements Paradoxically, the National Alliance’s (NA) biggest problem at the moment is that many of the issues the party has championed in Latvian politics for years – the transition to Latvian as the language of education and the public sphere, a much tougher stance towards Russia, higher defence spending, the removal of the Soviet legacy and an increasingly cautious approach to immigration – are no longer exclusively NA issues. To varying degrees, they have also been adopted by other political forces. Although the ratings suggest that some National Alliance voters have moved to other political forces – from 9.4% in the 14th Saeima election to 4.5% in the SKDS poll this August – the party still has its own loyal voters, some of whom have supported it since the days of the slogan “Latvian, don’t give up!” For years, NA sought to make Latvian politics more Latvian-oriented, more firmly opposed to Russia, tougher on security issues and more cautious towards immigration. These issues were important enough to the party’s voters for them to cast their ballots specifically for the nationalists. Traditionally, NA has been a political force with a “core electorate”. Yet, as the decline in its ratings suggests, part of that electorate has now become less loyal to the party. Why? National-conservative rhetoric centred on sovereignty, family values and strict migration policies is now being offered in various combinations by several other candidate lists. This means that voters who consider these values important no longer have to choose NA. The party must therefore compete with other political forces operating in the right-wing nationalist and socially conservative political space. Advertisements Leaders of the party’s candidate lists NA is heading into the 15th Saeima election without Raivis Dzintars, a politician with whom the party had been closely associated since the establishment of the National Alliance “All for Latvia! – For Fatherland and Freedom/LNNK” in 2010. In this election, Ilze Indriksone is the party’s candidate for prime minister and heads its Riga list. Jānis Dombrava is number one in Vidzeme, Jānis Vitenbergs heads the Zemgale list, Artūrs Butāns leads the Kurzeme list, and Edmunds Teirumnieks is number one in Latgale. As Minister of Education and Science, Ilze Indriksone inherited a difficult portfolio – the issue of raising teachers’ salaries, disputes surrounding general education reform, proposals to tighten requirements for foreign students, and other challenges. Advertisements Jānis Dombrava is positioned as NA’s leading politician on migration and national security. The Ministry of the Interior regularly highlights its minister’s achievements, recalling Operation VILKATIS on the Latvia–Belarus border, expanded video surveillance capabilities for border guards, the beginning of work to introduce State Defence Service within the State Border Guard, and other measures. Vitenbergs has ministerial experience at the Ministry of Economics, the Ministry of Transport and now the Ministry of Climate and Energy. He has identified the security of energy infrastructure, readiness for the heating season and improving the business environment as his main priorities. Artūrs Butāns is one of the most visible politicians of NA’s younger generation and clearly one of the figures on whom the party is building its post-Dzintars era. Edmunds Teirumnieks, who holds a doctorate in engineering and is a professor and leading researcher at the RTU Rēzekne Academy, is more closely associated with regional development, higher education and the interests of Latgale. Advertisements Culture Minister Nauris Puntulis, who is running as number two on the Riga list, has long personified NA’s cultural policy. Ināra Mūrniece, meanwhile, who is running as number two in Vidzeme, brings the party the experience of a former Saeima Speaker and defence minister, and currently chairs the Saeima Foreign Affairs Committee. At European level, the party also still has Roberts Zīle – one of NA’s longest-serving and most internationally recognisable political figures. From ideology to social and economic issues The party promises the right to receive any service in Latvian in both the public and private sectors, greater powers for the State Language Centre and a Latvian “derussification declaration”. Advertisements In the field of security, NA proposes spending more than 5% of GDP on defence, developing Latvia’s domestic military industry, strengthening air-defence, drone and counter-drone capabilities, and increasing the number of trained reservists. Its offer to families is also quite attractive. NA promises to increase the childcare allowance to 600 euros and index it, while setting the state family benefit at 100 euros for one child, 300 euros for two children and 600 euros for three or more children. The party also promises fully state-funded healthcare for children, partial cancellation of student loans after the birth of a child, a 15,000-euro grant to reduce a mortgage for each child, and state-guaranteed housing loans for young families without a down payment. This fits well with the party’s traditional identity politics: if Latvia wants more Latvians living in Latvia, the state should provide families with as much support as possible to encourage them to have more children. Advertisements Yet no matter how attractive election promises may sound, fiscal and political reality tends to bring dreamers back down to earth after an election. First, there is a significant difference between making promises and securing the funding required to fulfil them. Parties would therefore be well advised to explain where they intend to find the money, particularly at a time when the state is simultaneously promising more funding for defence, healthcare, internal security and other sectors. Second, it should not be forgotten that political decisions are made through compromise, dictated by coalition dynamics, the aforementioned budget constraints and unforeseen crises such as the Covid pandemic or geopolitical conflicts. And finally, there are populism and bureaucracy. Family policy is unlikely to be an issue that any party would actively oppose, but no one has abolished bureaucratic foot-dragging. Advertisements The hot potato – migration Migration is the hot potato that the governing coalition is currently tossing from hand to hand, without quite knowing what to do with it during the election campaign. On the one hand, part of society demands restrictions on virtually any form of immigration and is concerned about the associated security risks. On the other hand, there is a growing demand for labour that is becoming increasingly difficult to meet without employing third-country nationals. NA’s position is aimed at reducing immigration as much as possible, while its ideological opponents on values and social policy – the Progressives – oppose a migration policy based on “prejudice, racism and fear of those who are different”. Advertisements ZZS, meanwhile, points to the need to address labour shortages in Latvia’s economy and therefore supports controlled “labour migration”. New Unity holds a similar position. It is also worth recalling that Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs of the United List blocked Interior Minister Jānis Dombrava’s migration restriction plan at a government meeting, describing it, among other things, as “political theatre” and an attempt to mislead voters. From an election campaign perspective, however, this conflict gives NA an opportunity to demonstrate that although it is part of the government, it maintains a firm position on issues that matter to the party and its voters. In other words, the old “strong backbone” meme associated with NA’s predecessor, For Fatherland and Freedom/LNNK, and its positioning as the party most ideologically consistent on national issues have not disappeared. Advertisements Strict migration controls therefore fit NA’s traditional identity. At the same time, employers’ arguments about labour shortages, universities’ interest in attracting foreign students – and their money – as well as EU legal constraints remain relevant to a significant part of society. In August, when migration had already become one of NA’s central political issues, the party’s rating in the SKDS poll fell from 5.5% to 4.5%. This alone does not prove a causal relationship between the party’s position on migration and the decline in support among potential voters. Nevertheless, there is a considerable possibility that the more moderate section of NA’s electorate has turned away from the party precisely because of its consistent strategy of restricting migration. What the ratings show Advertisements The National Alliance spent almost the entire 14th Saeima term alternating between being a governing party and an opposition force. Following the 2022 election, NA was part of Krišjānis Kariņš’ government, but after Evika Siliņa formed her government in 2023, the party moved into opposition. As a result, NA spent most of the parliamentary term outside government and was able to enjoy the politically convenient advantage of criticising virtually any government decision without having to take responsibility for it itself. This may have been one of the reasons why NA recorded some of its strongest ratings during its period in opposition – 9.9% in the December 2024 SKDS poll and, after a slight decline in March and April, 9.7% in July 2025. Advertisements Last autumn, however, NA’s ratings began to fall sharply – from 9.7% in July to 6.4% in October and 5.6% in November. The political conflict surrounding the Istanbul Convention punched a major hole in NA’s support. In an SKDS poll, 40% of NA voters said Latvia should definitely withdraw from the Convention, while another 16% said it should probably withdraw. At the same time, 22% said Latvia should definitely remain in the Convention and another 9% said it should probably remain. Although the party consistently voted in favour of withdrawal, after the President decided to return the law to the Saeima for reconsideration, NA agreed to leave the final decision to the 15th Saeima. Advertisements NA explained this as a question of the timing of the vote rather than a change in its position. Nevertheless, it created a political risk of losing supporters from both camps. For NA’s more moderate and strongly pro-European voters, the very initiative to withdraw may have been unacceptable, while more firmly conservative voters could have viewed the compromise and postponement of the decision as insufficiently consistent. It should also be noted that a poll conducted by Latvijas Fakti in cooperation with Faktu logs between the 21st and the 31st of August showed support for NA at 7.3% of all respondents. While NA ranked fifth in the SKDS poll, it placed third in the Latvijas Fakti survey, where 23.1% of respondents remained undecided. However, the two polls are not directly comparable. SKDS and Latvijas Fakti use different methods to reach respondents, and such methodological differences can affect the results. Advertisements What is the bottom line? NA still has a recognisable ideology, experienced politicians, ministerial posts and a long-standing core electorate. However, its once clearly defined political niche has become crowded, while the values and positions that matter to nationally minded voters are increasingly being adopted by the party’s competitors within the same political space. On the more moderate side, NA faces competition for voters from Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs’ United List and, on certain issues, New Unity. ZZS, the New Conservative Party (JKP) and others are also competing for socially conservative, family-oriented voters. On the national-conservative side, there is also Rising Sun for Latvia (ASL), founded by Raivis Zeltīts after he left the National Alliance a year ago. ASL essentially offers the same ideology as NA, but in a much more radical form. ASL has little prospect of entering the 15th Saeima, but the roughly one percentage point of support it has attracted has most likely come at NA’s expense. Advertisements At this point, the main question is not whether NA will clear the 5% threshold required to enter the 15th Saeima. Both the SKDS and Latvijas Fakti ratings indicate that it will. The more important question is whether voters who care about the Latvian language, national security, a restrictive migration policy, demographics and a firm, critical stance towards Russia still regard the National Alliance as the principal political representative of those interests. It is precisely this political “ownership” of the national-conservative electorate that NA is now fighting to retain.
